title: The LORD Proclaims His Name and Renews the Covenant
summary: Moses cuts two new stone tablets and climbs Sinai again, and the LORD passes before him proclaiming his name: compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, forgiving, yet not leaving the guilty unpunished. God renews the covenant with commands against idolatry and for Israel's feasts and firstfruits. Moses comes down after forty days with his face shining, and afterward he veils it except when he speaks with God.
story: The covenant sealed in chapter 24 was shattered with the tablets in chapter 32. Chapter 33 ended with God's promise that his presence would go with Israel and that Moses would see his goodness pass by. Now that promise is kept. The golden calf episode ends not with Israel's repentance proving itself, but with God declaring who he is. The same God who had threatened to consume his people describes himself first as compassionate and gracious. On that basis the covenant is remade, the second set of tablets is written, and the work of building the tabernacle can begin in chapter 35. The self-description in verses 6 and 7 becomes Israel's creed about God, quoted and echoed across the rest of the Old Testament.
historical:
The setting is again the summit of Sinai, with the mountain sealed off as it was in chapter 19. The laws in verses 11 to 26 closely parallel the covenant laws of 23:12-19, and some critical scholars call this section the Ritual Decalogue, proposing that it preserved a different list of ten commandments. Verse 28 says the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments, were written on the tablets, and it is unclear in Hebrew whether he refers to Moses or to God; Deuteronomy 10:2-4 says the LORD wrote the same words that were on the first tablets. Most readers take the tablets to hold the Ten Commandments of chapter 20, with verses 10 to 26 as a restatement of key covenant duties after the calf.

The warnings against Canaanite worship reflect a real and lasting temptation. Asherah was a goddess known from the Ugaritic texts as the consort of the high god El, and her cult object, a wooden pole or stylized tree, stood at many shrines. Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai, from about 800 BC, bless people by the LORD and his asherah, which shows that some Israelites later combined the worship of the LORD with her. The month of Abib (verse 18) is an old name meaning fresh ears of grain, the season of barley harvest in spring; after the exile the Babylonian name Nisan took its place.
cultural:
Israel's worship was tied to the farming year. The Feast of Unleavened Bread came at the barley harvest in spring and remembered the exodus; the Feast of Weeks, later called Pentecost from the Greek word for fiftieth, marked the wheat harvest seven weeks later; and the Feast of Ingathering, also called Booths or Tabernacles, closed the year's harvest in autumn. At each one the men of Israel were to appear before God. Leaving farms and borders unguarded three times a year was an act of trust, which is why verse 24 promises that no one will covet their land while they are away. The firstborn of animals and sons belonged to God and had to be given or redeemed.

The command not to cook a young goat in its mother's milk (verse 26) appears three times in the Torah (23:19; Deuteronomy 14:21). Scholars once explained it as a ban on a Canaanite ritual known from a Ugaritic text, but that reading of the text is now widely doubted. Others see a moral lesson about not confusing the source of life with the means of death, alongside laws such as Deuteronomy 22:6-7. Rabbinic tradition built on this verse the Jewish practice of separating meat and dairy. The shining face of Moses had a curious later history: the Hebrew verb for shine is related to the word for horn, and the Latin Vulgate translated it as horned, which is why medieval and Renaissance art, including Michelangelo's statue of Moses in Rome, gives him horns.
literary: The chapter has three movements: the theophany and God's proclamation of his name (verses 1-9), the covenant renewal and its commands (verses 10-28), and Moses' descent with a shining face (verses 29-35). The proclamation of verses 6 and 7 is balanced with care: a long list of mercies and then a short, sober note of justice, with love extended to a thousand generations and punishment limited to three or four. It expands the words of 20:5-6, where the order was reversed and judgment came first. Its phrases reappear in Numbers 14:18, Nehemiah 9:17, Psalms 86:15, 103:8, and 145:8, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2, and Nahum 1:3. Jonah even complains about it: “I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion.”

outline.t: New tablets and a second ascent
The LORD proclaims his name, and Moses worships and pleads
The covenant renewed: no treaties and no other gods
The words of the covenant written
Moses' radiant face and the veil

doctrines.note: Asked to show his glory, God describes his character. Mercy, grace, patience, loyal love, faithfulness, and forgiveness come first and at length; justice comes last but is not removed. The Old Testament's most repeated statement about God holds love and justice together without letting either cancel the other.

The covenant is renewed after it has been broken, and the renewal rests on God's character rather than Israel's record. Moses' plea in verse 9 names the people as stiff-necked and asks for forgiveness on that very basis.

God's name is Jealous (verse 14): he claims Israel's exclusive worship as a husband claims his wife's faithfulness. The warnings against intermarriage and shared sacrifices concern the pull toward other gods, which verse 16 names directly.

words.note: Chesed, loving devotion, often translated steadfast love, lovingkindness, or loyal love. It is love that keeps faith within a relationship, especially when the other party has failed. Here God abounds in it and maintains it to a thousand generations. It is one of the Old Testament's great words for God's character.

Emet, faithfulness or truth. It describes what is firm and reliable; the related word amen comes from the same root. Paired with chesed, it means God's love is dependable. John's description of Jesus as full of grace and truth (John 1:14) probably echoes this pair.

Qanna, Jealous, used only of God in the Old Testament. It is not petty envy but the passionate, exclusive love that will not share a covenant partner with rivals. Here it is even called God's name, a way of saying this is essential to who he is.

Qaran, to shine or send out rays. The verb is related to the noun qeren, horn, and in the sense of shining it appears only in this passage. The link explains the old Latin rendering horned and the tradition of horned Moses in European art, but the sense in context is clearly that his skin shone from being in God's presence.

christ: John's Gospel draws on this chapter as it introduces Jesus. Moses asked to see God's glory and heard him proclaimed as abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness; John says of the Word made flesh, “We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), and adds, “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Paul reads the shining face and the veil in 2 Corinthians 3. He contrasts the glory of the covenant written on stone with the greater glory of the Spirit's ministry, and he says that believers, “who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Paul adds that the veil kept Israel from seeing the glory fading, a detail Exodus does not state, and interpreters differ on how he reached it. Moses' forty days without food on the mountain also find an echo in Jesus' forty days of fasting in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2).

hard.q: Does God punish children for their parents' sins?
hard.a:
Verse 7 says God visits the iniquity of the fathers on their children and grandchildren to the third and fourth generations. Read alone, it sounds like inherited guilt. Other texts rule that out as a principle of justice: “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father” (Ezekiel 18:20), and Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids executing children for their parents' crimes. Interpreters reconcile these in several ways. Many note that three or four generations is the size of a household living together at one time, so the verse describes how a family's sin damages everyone under its roof, rather than a curse on distant descendants. The parallel in 20:5 adds the words of those who hate Me, suggesting that later generations who continue in the same sin share its judgment. Some take verse 7 as a statement about national history, where the consequences of a people's sin carry forward.

The proportion also matters. Love reaches to a thousand generations; judgment stops at three or four. The verse is part of a proclamation whose main point is God's mercy. Jesus rejected the assumption that a man was born blind because of his parents' sin (John 9:2-3), which shows that the verse was not to be used to explain every suffering.

questions: When Moses asked to see God's glory, God described his character. Which part of verses 6 and 7 do you find hardest to believe about God, and why?
Jonah was angry that God was gracious to his enemies. Whom would you be uncomfortable seeing God forgive?
Moses did not know his face was shining. What does it suggest that the effects of time with God may be more visible to others than to ourselves?
